meta.title: Who really said "Money Can't Buy Love, But It Improves Your Bargaining Position"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Christopher Marlowe, who died in 1593. The quip dates to 1954, and the Marlowe credit is a misread parenthesis in a 1977 quotation book.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Money Can't Buy Love, But It Improves Your Bargaining Position'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Christopher Marlowe. It is an anonymous 1954 newspaper quip, and the Marlowe credit comes from a misread parenthesis in a 1977 book.

answer.label: Not Christopher Marlowe — an anonymous 1954 quip
answer.sourceLine: Marlowe died in 1593, and nothing like this appears in his work — Quote Investigator checked his one famous poem about love, The Passionate Shepherd to His Love, which does not mention money or bargaining. The earliest instance QI located is an unsigned item in The Elgin Echo of Elgin, Iowa, on 18 March 1954, worded “Money cannot buy love, but it places one in an excellent bargaining position.” The exact modern phrasing appears in 1977 as a parenthetical that the editor Laurence J. Peter wrote into Peter’s Quotations — and that is where the Marlowe credit was born, by misreading the page.

source.heading: The earliest printing

source.excerpt: Money cannot buy love, but it places one in an excellent bargaining position.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ is the anchor. Its conclusion: “this comical remark was in circulation by 1954, and initially it was anonymous.”

QI reconstructs how Marlowe’s name got attached. In Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time (1977), page 309, the saying appears in parentheses between a Henry S. Haskins quotation and a Christopher Marlowe quotation. QI states the parenthetical “was written and inserted by the editor Laurence J. Peter though he did not originate the statement”, and hypothesises that readers “incorrectly decided to ascribe the expression between parentheses to Christopher Marlowe”.

The mis-reading then propagated into print: QI documents The Mammoth Book of Great British Humor crediting Marlowe in 2010, and Robert C. Solomon’s Love: Emotion, Myth, and Metaphor crediting Laurence J. Peter in 1981 — two different wrong answers from the same page.
Marlowe’s dates, 1564 to 1593, are confirmed against his Wikipedia entry ↗, which puts him three and a half centuries before the earliest known printing.
source.excerptNote: The 1954 Elgin Echo wording, as Quote Investigator transcribes it — the earliest instance located, and unattributed. Evan Esar printed a closer variant in 20,000 Quips and Quotes in 1968: “Money cannot buy love, but it can put you in a good bargaining position.”

author.name: Christopher Marlowe
author.heading: About Christopher Marlowe
author.metaLine: 1564–1593 · English playwright, poet and translator of the Elizabethan era
author.bio: Christopher Marlowe (1564–1593) was an English playwright and poet of the Elizabethan era, author of Doctor Faustus, Tamburlaine and The Jew of Malta, and a decisive influence on Shakespeare. He died at twenty-nine. His best-known poem about love, The Passionate Shepherd to His Love, is an invitation to pastoral pleasures and mentions neither money nor bargaining — and the quip credited to him here was not printed anywhere until 1954.

The modern wording appears as an editorial parenthetical in Laurence J. Peter, Peter’s Quotations: Ideas for Our Time (New York: William Morrow, 1977), 309.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two names circulate, and both come from the same page of the same 1977 book — one by misreading its typography, the other by over-reading its editor’s role.

items.why: Marlowe died in 1593, some 361 years before the earliest documented printing. QI traces the credit ↗ to readers of Peter’s Quotations (1977) attaching the parenthetical above Marlowe’s name to Marlowe himself.

items.tag: Worded it, did not originate it
items.why: Peter (1919–1990) did write the parenthetical as it appears in his 1977 compilation, and some collections credit him — Robert C. Solomon’s 1981 book among them. But QI is explicit ↗ that “he did not originate the statement”: it was already circulating in 1954.

Esar included “Money cannot buy love, but it can put you in a good bargaining position” in 20,000 Quips and Quotes in 1968, under “Love and Money”. That is nine years before Peter’s book and fourteen after the Iowa newspaper — a waypoint in the drift, not an origin.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s verdict ↗: anonymous, in circulation by 1954. The honest credit is unknown.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is the cleanest example in the corpus of a misattribution produced by page layout rather than by anybody’s claim. Nobody ever asserted Marlowe said it. A 1977 editor put his own aside in brackets, the next quotation down happened to be Marlowe’s, and a generation of readers drew the obvious wrong line between them.

What makes it stick is that the joke sounds Elizabethan-adjacent — worldly, cynical, epigrammatic — so the credit never felt absurd enough to check. It is, in fact, a gag from an Iowa newspaper column called “Pipe Dreams”.
context.pull: Nobody ever asserted Marlowe said it. A bracket and a line break did it for them.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the remark was in circulation by 1954 and was initially anonymous.

QI gives the earliest instance as The Elgin Echo, Elgin, Iowa, 18 March 1954, quote page 2 column 1, in a humour column, worded 'Money cannot buy love, but it places one in an excellent bargaining position' with no attribution.

QI states the parenthetical in Peter's Quotations (1977), page 309, was written and inserted by the editor Laurence J. Peter though he did not originate the statement, and hypothesises readers mis-ascribed it to Christopher Marlowe because a Marlowe quotation followed it on the page.
QI records Evan Esar's 1968 variant in 20,000 Quips and Quotes, page 492, reading 'Money cannot buy love, but it can put you in a good bargaining position.'

QI notes Marlowe's The Passionate Shepherd to His Love does not discuss money or bargaining, and documents the 2010 Mammoth Book of Great British Humor crediting Marlowe and Robert C. Solomon's 1981 book crediting Laurence J. Peter.
Christopher Marlowe was an English playwright and poet who lived 1564 to 1593.
Laurence J. Peter was a Canadian educator who lived 1919 to 1990 and is best known for The Peter Principle.
